project.topic: What if every active volcano on Earth erupted at once?
project.title: What if every active volcano on Earth erupted at once?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If every active volcano erupted at the same moment, is the danger the lava and ash near the mountains, or something that reaches everyone?
project.viewer_takeaway: Lava and ash are deadly but local; the sulfur that the biggest eruptions lift into the stratosphere dims the sun for about a year, cooling summers and threatening harvests far from any volcano, as Tambora did in 1816.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: About 1,350 volcanoes are potentially active; roughly 50-70 erupt in a typical year, most of them small. Only a few large explosive eruptions per century lift enough sulfur into the stratosphere to cool the climate.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: Every potentially active volcano starts an eruption at the same moment, each one typical of what that volcano does. Weather, oceans and people are otherwise unchanged. The film follows one city 15.7 km from a stratovolcano, then the planet over the following year.
assumptions: Each volcano produces an eruption typical for itself: most small, a minority large and explosive.
Only large explosive eruptions reach the stratosphere (about 15-25 km).
The street, the city and its volcano are illustrative; distances are typical of cities near volcanoes.
Local readings on the HUD (time, lava and ash-flow speeds, ash depth, air temperatures) are illustrative values for the scenes shown.
causal_chain: All active volcanoes erupt at once.
Near the mountains, lava is usually slow but pyroclastic flows and ashfall are deadly; about 800 million people live within 100 km of an active volcano.
Ash falls out of the air within hours to days.
Sulfur dioxide from the largest blasts reaches the stratosphere, becomes sulfate droplets, spreads around the globe in weeks and stays for about a year.
The droplets reflect sunlight, cooling the surface; Tambora (1815) caused the 1816 Year Without a Summer.
All eruptions together could inject more than Tambora, so northern summers and harvests could fail, and cooling is felt worldwide.
uncertainties: How much sulfur all eruptions together would inject depends on how many large explosive eruptions occur: anywhere from about one Pinatubo to several Tamboras.
Cooling is uneven: strongest over northern continents in summer, weaker in the tropics and southern oceans.
Food-system outcomes depend on stocks, trade and adaptation.

claims.statement: There are about 1,350 potentially active volcanoes on Earth (excluding mid-ocean ridges); the scenario has all of them erupt at once.
claims.reasoning: USGS count; the simultaneity is the stipulated premise.
claims.presentation_guardrail: The HUD count is the premise, not a forecast.

claims.statement: About 800 million people live within 100 km of an active volcano.
claims.reasoning: Brown et al. (2015), Global Volcanic Hazards and Risk.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Within 100 km does not mean every person is hit by ash flows.

claims.statement: Most lava flows advance slowly enough for people to walk away, while pyroclastic flows move at roughly 80 to over 400 km/h and can outrun vehicles.
claims.reasoning: USGS Volcano Hazards Program descriptions of lava flows and pyroclastic flows.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Some fluid lava flows are fast; "most" stays in the line.

claims.statement: Volcanic ash falls out of the atmosphere within hours to days, mostly near the volcano.
claims.reasoning: Ash particles are heavy; NOAA notes the gas, not the ash, drives global effects.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Fine ash can drift far and disrupt aviation for days.

claims.statement: Large explosive eruptions inject sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, where it forms sulfate droplets that spread around the globe within weeks, persist for about a year or two and reflect sunlight, cooling the surface (Pinatubo 1991: about 15-20 Mt SO2, about 0.5-0.6 °C).
claims.reasoning: NASA Earth Observatory and NOAA summaries of Pinatubo and volcanic aerosols.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Only the biggest blasts reach the stratosphere.

claims.statement: Tambora (April 1815) released about 53-58 Mt of SO2; 1816 became the Year Without a Summer, with snow in New England in June 1816 and widespread crop failures.
claims.reasoning: Self et al. (2004); historical records summarised by Raible et al. (2016).
claims.presentation_guardrail: Global cooling about 0.4-0.8 °C; regional summer cooling larger.

claims.statement: If every active volcano erupted at once, the large explosive eruptions among them could together inject more stratospheric sulfur than Tambora.
claims.reasoning: Long-dormant volcanoes tend to produce larger eruptions; if even a few of the ~1,350 produced Pinatubo-sized eruptions (15-20 Mt each) the total would pass Tambora. A purely typical-year mix would give about one Pinatubo.

claims.statement: Cooling of that size could bring summer frosts and failed harvests across northern mid-latitudes, as in 1816.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Food outcomes depend on stocks and trade.

claims.statement: The cooling would be global but uneven: lava and ash stay regional, the temperature drop reaches every continent.
claims.reasoning: Stratospheric aerosol spreads globally; tropical and ocean regions cool less.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "The cold reaches everyone" means a measurable global drop, not winter everywhere.

creative_direction.logline: The volcano down your street erupts along with every other one on Earth; the ash ends in days, but the sulfur dims the sun and the cold spreads to everyone.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Grounded eye-level street views of a towering ash column, a hot flank road, a daytime-dark ash fall, then a pale milky sun; orbit shots of glowing volcanic belts and a spreading white veil; snow and frost on June farms.
creative_direction.lighting: Low morning sun on the column; daytime darkness under ash with street lamps; milky high haze with a whitish sun; overcast snow light; hazy orange dawn.
creative_direction.camera_language: Handheld eye-level street and road views (1.5-1.6 m) with an impulse at the blast wave; slow orbits for the planet; a tilt from your broom to the dim sun.
creative_direction.motion_language: Real-speed physics: a slowly rising column, creeping lava, a fast ash flow, steady ash fall, a veil spreading over weeks in time-lapse.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: Metre scale on the ground with the volcano at true size and distance; Earth radius 1 for orbit shots with eruption points and the veil exaggerated for legibility.
creative_direction.opening_hook: The mountain down your street just exploded. It's not the only one.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: When the ash is swept away the danger seems over, but the sun stays dim: sulfur from the biggest blasts hangs 20 km up for a year, bouncing sunlight back to space.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: The lava and ash stay near the mountains; the cold reaches everyone.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The last shot returns to the opening view down your street, now under a pale sun with the volcano quiet.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the street, volcano, globe, humanoids, grass, trees, houses and snow; add a reusable eruption-column-v1 (Plinian column, umbrella cloud and pyroclastic flow).

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original score: low drones and distant thunder for the eruption, a cold airy pad for the haze, sparse piano and a resolving chord for the ending.
audio.sfx_direction: 0.3 s silence then the blast wave with rattling windows; crackling lava crust; roaring ash flow and a passing car; ash hiss on umbrellas; broom on ash; muffled snow; frost crunch.
